Empiricism is the position that all knowledge comes ultimately from sensory experience, not from innate ideas or pure reason. Emerging in seventeenth and eighteenth-century Britain through John Locke, David Hume, and John Stuart Mill, empiricism insists that the mind begins as a blank slate, a tabula rasa, and that complex ideas are built from simple impressions through association and reflection. These philosophers challenged the rationalist confidence in deduction and in knowledge that is knowable before experience, arguing instead that knowledge of the world comes through careful observation and inductive reasoning.

The foundations of empiricism rest on several key thinkers. John Locke, living from sixteen thirty-two to seventeen hundred and four, argued against innate ideas, claiming that all knowledge begins in sensation and reflection on experience. David Hume, from seventeen eleven to seventeen seventy-six, radicalized empiricism by arguing that causation, induction, and even personal identity have no rational foundation but are habits of mind. John Stuart Mill, from eighteen hundred and six to eighteen seventy-three, extended empiricism to logic and mathematics, arguing that even mathematical truths derive ultimately from patterns found in experience.

Empiricism rests on several core doctrines. The mind is blank at birth, a tabula rasa, and all ideas enter through the senses. Simple impressions combine to form complex thoughts; reason is rearrangement, not creation. Knowledge of the world proceeds through observation and generalization, not through deductive axioms. Empiricists were skeptical about metaphysics—propositions not grounded in experience, such as claims about God or the soul or causal necessity, are cognitively empty. Hume showed that induction itself cannot be rationally justified, a persistent epistemological challenge. Only particulars, this red apple for instance, are real; universals like redness or appleness are mental constructs, a view called nominalism.

Empiricism crystallized as a reaction against rationalism's confidence in deduction and innate knowledge, and it aligned philosophy with the emerging scientific method practiced by Boyle and Newton. Hume's radical critique of induction and causation exposed deep problems in both empiricism and rationalism, eventually leading to Kant's critical response. Empiricism became the dominant Anglo-American philosophical tradition and undergirds modern epistemology and philosophy of science, with its emphasis on observation and testability prefiguring logical positivism.
